_comment: Labels for the 31 links in macrosim_model_v1.json. Keys are link ids. 'label' is the bar label in the attribution panel; 'plain' is the one-line explanation under it.

r_to_gexp.label: Policy rate
r_to_gexp.plain: A higher rate is expected to slow the economy, so growth expectations are marked down straight away.

cred_to_gexp.label: Credit conditions
cred_to_gexp.plain: Easier credit today makes faster growth look more likely.

supply_to_gexp.label: Energy supply
supply_to_gexp.plain: A supply shock is a tax on activity, so expected growth falls.

g_to_gexp.label: Current growth
g_to_gexp.plain: Expectations start from what the economy is already doing.

pi_to_piexp.label: Current inflation
pi_to_piexp.plain: People expect roughly what they are already living through.

supply_to_piexp.label: Energy supply
supply_to_piexp.plain: A supply shock is expected to feed straight into prices.

gexp_to_piexp.label: Expected growth
gexp_to_piexp.plain: A hotter economy is expected to push prices up.

r_to_piexp.label: Policy rate
r_to_piexp.plain: A central bank willing to raise rates is expected to hold inflation down.

r_to_y.label: Policy rate
r_to_y.plain: The long rate follows the short rate, but only about seventy percent of the way.

piexp_to_y.label: Expected inflation
piexp_to_y.plain: Lenders want compensating for the inflation they expect.

gexp_to_y.label: Expected growth
gexp_to_y.plain: Weaker expected growth pulls the long rate back down.

r_to_usd.label: Policy rate
r_to_usd.plain: Higher rates pay investors more to hold the currency.

gexp_to_usd.label: Expected growth
gexp_to_usd.plain: A stronger economy attracts money; a weaker one repels it.

supply_to_usd.label: Energy supply
supply_to_usd.plain: A small safe-haven bid when the physical economy is disrupted.

supply_to_e.label: Supply shock
supply_to_e.plain: The shock itself. Exogenous, immediate, and held until it is changed.

g_to_e.label: Demand
g_to_e.plain: A growing economy burns more energy, a quarter or two later.

usd_to_e.label: Dollar
usd_to_e.plain: Energy is priced in dollars, so a stronger dollar makes it cheaper the same quarter.

r_to_cred.label: Policy rate
r_to_cred.plain: The main brake. A higher rate tightens lending, starting the quarter after the decision.

g_to_cred.label: Growth
g_to_cred.plain: Lenders lend more readily into a growing economy.

usd_to_cred.label: Dollar
usd_to_cred.plain: A stronger dollar tightens conditions for everyone holding dollar debt.

cred_to_g.label: Credit
cred_to_g.plain: The main channel from rates to the real economy. Tighter credit, less spending and investment.

e_to_g.label: Energy
e_to_g.plain: Expensive energy is a cost on every producer and a bill for every household.

eq_to_g.label: Equities
eq_to_g.plain: The wealth effect. When portfolios fall, people spend less even if wages have not changed.

pi_ar.label: Persistence
pi_ar.plain: Half of last quarter's inflation gap carries over. Prices have memory, which is why a cost shock fades slowly.

e_to_pi.label: Energy
e_to_pi.plain: Energy costs reach the shelf from the next quarter onward.

g_to_pi.label: Demand
g_to_pi.plain: The Phillips channel. A hot economy lifts prices, but only after about three quarters.

usd_to_pi.label: Dollar
usd_to_pi.plain: A stronger dollar makes imports cheaper, with a long lag.

y_to_eq.label: Discount rate
y_to_eq.plain: The measuring stick. A higher yield makes future profits worth less today, whatever those profits turn out to be.

gexp_to_eq.label: Expected profits
gexp_to_eq.plain: Shares are a claim on future profits, so expected growth moves them directly.

cred_to_eq.label: Credit conditions
cred_to_eq.plain: Easier credit supports valuations. It carries a one-quarter lag, so it contributes nothing in a shock quarter.

e_to_eq.label: Energy costs
e_to_eq.plain: Expensive energy eats margins across the market.
